panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Axial pre-Furosemide MRI shows a dilated right renal pelvis in a pediatric patient with known right UPJO; caption documents pelvic AP diameter measurement. B: Post-Furosemide axial MRI shows persistent right pelvicalyceal dilatation with measured AP diameter, consistent with UPJO. C: Coronal post-contrast MR angiographic sequence demonstrates the accessory lower pole renal artery crossing the right UPJ, the stated cause of UPJO. D: Coronal urographic-phase MRI shows delayed right-sided excretion compared with the left side, consistent with obstruction at the UPJ, with visible right pelvicalyceal dilatation.

panels.rationale: Single axial noncontrast CT of the right kidney in a real patient. The caption and article title identify occult congenital ureteropelvic junction obstruction; the image shows a markedly hydronephrotic renal pelvis, severe cortical atrophy, and urine extravasation/rupture, supporting UPJ obstruction with its CT manifestations. Presentation with collecting system rupture after blunt trauma is atypical.

Also noted was a defect in the right renal pelvis, which was severely dilated and associated with severe right cortical atrophy (Fig. 1). These findings were consistent with a Grade IV renal trauma according to the Revised Renal Injury Staging Classification.7 There were no other traumatic findings of the abdomen and pelvis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Axial CT panel from a patient with silent ureteropelvic junction obstruction; caption describes mild fullness of the left renal pelvis, consistent with early hydronephrosis. Article title and in-text context support UPJO attribution. B: Axial CT panel one year later shows marked left hydronephrosis with cortical thinning, a classic manifestation of ureteropelvic junction obstruction in the same patient.

Indian journal of urology : IJU : journal of the Urological Society of India 2009. doi:10.4103/0970-1591.45553. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: A. Initial CT scan. Note mild fullness of left renal pelvis. B. CT scan one year later. Note marked hydronephrosis of left kidney with thinning of renal parenchyma.
in_text_mentions: A 62-year-old woman was referred for a brief episode of left flank pain and imaging demonstrating fullness of the left renal pelvis [Figure 1A]. She had no prior urologic history of colic, urolithiasis, or infection. Her serum creatinine was 1.0 mg/dl and urine culture was negative for bacteriuria. She was further evaluated with a MAG-3 diuretic renal scan demonstrating symmetric renal function and no evidence of left-sided obstruction (T ½ of 6 min) after administration of a diuretic [Figure 2A]. She was discharged from our clinic and instructed to return if she experienced further symptoms.

request of her primary care physician, the patient underwent repeat computed tomography (CT) imaging 12 months later despite being asymptomatic. Repeat imaging demonstrated severe left-sided hydronephrosis [Figure 1B]. Repeat nuclear renography at that time demonstrated loss of renal function from 50 to 10% [Figure 2B]. The patient then underwent placement of a left ureteral stent with no improvement in differential renal function on renography four weeks later. She subsequently elected for ureteral stent removal and has not had any repeated symptoms related to her UPJO at 6 months follow-up.

in_text_mentions: The mean renal pelvis diameter at the time of surgery was 25.6 (range 11–48 mm) mm and the mean function of the involved renal moiety was 28.3% before surgery. panels.rationale: Single-image non-contrast CT of a real patient showing a massively dilated right renal pelvis, a classic manifestation of ureteropelvic junction obstruction. The article title and in-text explicitly attribute the presentation to de novo UPJ obstruction, and the caption describes the dilated renal pelvis containing a large hematoma. Red arrows annotate the region. The hematoma is an atypical complication but the disease attribution is supported by the dilated renal pelvis.

panels.figure_caption: Non-contrast CT scan (sagittal view) through the level of the right kidney showing a large hematoma contained by a massively dilated renal pelvis (red arrows).
in_text_mentions: The patient represented to the ER 20 hours following discharge having been found cold and clammy at home - he was obtunded, hypotensive, and tachycardic. His relatives reported that his hematuria had recommenced and continued overnight. At presentation, his hemoglobin was noted to have dropped to 8.0 g/dl. Emergency contrast CT scan showed a grossly dilated right renal pelvis with a large contained hematoma. On imaging, there was no readily apparent cause of bleeding, nor were there any crossing vessels (Figures 1, 2).

in_text_mentions: The patient represented to the ER 20 hours following discharge having been found cold and clammy at home - he was obtunded, hypotensive, and tachycardic. His relatives reported that his hematuria had recommenced and continued overnight. At presentation, his hemoglobin was noted to have dropped to 8.0 g/dl. Emergency contrast CT scan showed a grossly dilated right renal pelvis with a large contained hematoma. On imaging, there was no readily apparent cause of bleeding, nor were there any crossing vessels (Figures 1, 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (Left panel, Right panel). Left panel: Real-patient retrograde pyelogram (radiograph) of a case of horseshoe kidney with right-sided UPJ obstruction; the arrow marks the right UPJO with a dilated, ballooned renal pelvis and abrupt pelviureteric tapering, classic pyelographic manifestations of ureteropelvic junction obstruction. Right panel: Same real-patient retrograde pyelogram showing a horseshoe kidney (white arrow marks the isthmus at L3) with dilated opacified pelves in the setting of documented right-sided UPJ obstruction; the caption's arrow specifically identifies the horseshoe isthmus rather than the obstruction itself, so the UPJO attribution rests on the dilated renal pelvis visible in this patient with confirmed UPJO, and confidence is correspondingly lower.
